script: How do solar panels turn sunlight into electricity? Let us take it step by step. A solar panel is made of many small cells, usually built from a material called silicon. Silicon is a semiconductor, which means it can carry electricity under the right conditions. When sunlight hits a solar cell, tiny particles of light called photons knock electrons loose from the silicon atoms. The cell is built with two layers that push these free electrons in one direction. That steady flow of electrons is an electric current. Thin metal lines on the surface of the cell collect this current and send it out through wires. But there is a catch. The electricity that comes out of a panel is direct current, while most homes use alternating current. So a box called an inverter converts it into the kind of power your lights and fridge can use. On a sunny day, a home system can produce more power than the family needs. The extra power can charge a battery for the evening, or flow back into the grid for neighbours to use. Panels work best when they face the sun and are kept free of dust and shade. Even on cloudy days, they still produce some power, just less. A typical panel keeps working for twenty five years or more, with very little maintenance. Today, solar power is one of the cheapest ways to produce electricity in many parts of the world. From rooftops in busy cities to large solar farms in the desert, the same simple idea is at work. Sunlight in, electricity out, and no smoke along the way.
